**Question:** why can the same pH leave one nitrogen base mainly neutral and
another mainly protonated?

Use this activity for about **8 minutes**: predict for 2 minutes, explore for
4, then explain your result for 2.

```{=html}
<section class="chem-demo" id="day18" aria-label="Amine protonation and molecular-species explorer">
<p>Enable JavaScript to compare the supplied molecular species and aqueous ionisation model.</p>
</section>
<script src="../interactives/core.js"></script>
<script src="../interactives/applications.js"></script>
```

### Predict

The supplied approximate aqueous conjugate-acid pKa values are methylammonium
**10.6**, anilinium **4.6**, and pyridinium **5.2**. For a base B and its
conjugate acid BH⁺,

$$f_{BH^+}=\frac{1}{1+10^{pH-pK_a}}.$$

Before moving a control, predict the fraction BH⁺ at pH = pKa and at one pH
unit below it. Predict which base is most protonated at pH 7.

### Explore

1. Use **At supplied pKa** for each molecule. Explain the common midpoint.
2. Compare all three molecules at pH 7 while keeping the environmental pH fixed.
3. For one molecule, move pH two units upward. Follow both the curve and the
   drawn neutral/protonated molecular forms.
4. Use **Reset** to reconstruct the original state.

### Explain and check

At pH = pKa, half the population is BH⁺. One unit below gives
$1/(1+0.1)=10/11$, about **90.9%**. At pH 7, methylamine is much more
protonated than aniline or pyridine under this model. Higher pH decreases
BH⁺, because deprotonated B becomes favoured.

A 50% fraction describes two populations of molecular species; it does not
mean that every nitrogen has half a proton. The ring drawings use implicit
carbon/hydrogen conventions; the N–H count and charge are shown explicitly.

### Model limits

These are supplied, approximate compatible **aqueous** pKa values in a dilute
one-site model. Substituents, solvent, temperature and activities can alter
behaviour. The plot predicts neither extraction recovery nor the rate of a
nucleophilic reaction. See the local [nitrogen exercises](../amines-aromatics/exercise.qmd)
for lone-pair and charge explanations.
